ai-at-work.title: Trump says he’s planning to create an ‘AI Force’ and hire a new AI czar
ai-at-work.excerpt: U.S. President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he is going to establish an “AI Force” and will also appoint a new AI czar, while dismissing concerns raised about the potential dangers of artificial
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Trump announced plans to create an "AI Force" and appoint an AI czar while dismissing AI safety concerns as a hoax. Digital workplace leaders need to pay attention because government AI policy directly shapes what tools, regulations, and workforce strategies will actually be available to us in the next few years. Here's the thing: whether you think this is great or terrible, one AI czar isn't going to solve the messy reality that most organizations are still figuring out how to use AI without accidentally firing their best people or creating legal nightmares.

ai-at-work.dwp_take: Stripe is buying OpenRouter, a dynamic model routing platform that intelligently directs AI requests to different large language models based on cost and performance. Digital workplace pros need to pay attention because this tech will reshape how companies deploy AI tools across their workforce, affecting everything from chatbot reliability to cloud spending. Here's the thing: after decades of watching IT chase the latest shiny object, I'll believe enterprises actually implement smart routing instead of just throwing everything at GPT-4 when I see it happen at scale.

ai-at-work.title: Why AI inference must become a commodity
ai-at-work.excerpt: The future of artificial intelligence inference isn’t premium; it’s ubiquitous and commoditized. That may sound odd coming from someone in the AI semiconductor business. Conventional wisdom suggests c
ai-at-work.dwp_take:
Here's my take:

AI inference costs are dropping fast enough that it'll soon be as cheap and standard as computing power itself. This matters to workplace tech because it means AI features won't be locked behind expensive enterprise licensing deals anymore, so your tools will actually get smarter without your CFO having a heart attack. The irony here is delicious: the people selling you AI chips are basically saying "buy our stuff so it becomes worthless," but they're right because adoption at scale beats fat margins every time.

ai-at-work.title: Salesforce after Dreamforce: How the CRM giant can grow beyond its own interface
ai-at-work.excerpt: Salesforce Inc.’s next growth opportunity just may come from customers spending less time in its interface, and having artificial intelligence agents do more of the work. Coming out of the customer re
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Salesforce is betting its future growth on AI agents handling more CRM work so users spend less time actually using Salesforce's interface. This matters because it signals a major shift in how enterprise platforms will operate, which means digital workplace leaders need to start thinking about AI-driven automation differently than they have been. Here's the thing though: if Salesforce succeeds, they'll have built a product people don't need to use much, which is either genius or the most ironic business model I've seen in three decades.

industry-news.title: Hackers Crack Flock Camera, Expose 1.6M Images in 21 Days
industry-news.excerpt: Hackers physically compromised a Flock camera and found an encryption key, 27,000 clips, and 1.6 million images generated in 21 days. The post Hackers Crack Flock Camera, Expose 1.6M Images in 21 Days
industry-news.dwp_take: Researchers physically accessed a Flock traffic camera, extracted its encryption key, and dumped 1.6 million images plus 27,000 video clips in just three weeks. This matters to workplace security teams because it shows that networked devices on your premises, even ones you think are "just cameras," can become serious breach vectors if physical security is sloppy. The real kicker here is that we spend billions on firewalls while leaving the actual hardware sitting on poles with worse security than a bicycle lock.
